doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Roy Halee calls him to play piano for Artie Garfunkel
summary: Years later Roy Halee hired him to play on Garfunkel's Old Man because of Lonesome Suzie.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Well I’ve got to tell you that what happened from that, you know, after we did the album and I left the band a year later in ’72, I was with them ’67 to ’71. A year later Roy Halee that was Simon & Garfunkel’s producer, they asked him to be producer on “Bridge Over Troubled Water” and some other stuff. Not all the albums, but he was an engineer. He was a great engineer and he was a trumpet player too. Classical. I didn’t know that. He was the first one to double the horns, great ears, great enthusiasm, he was like riding a bronco or something for the next lick that we play or anything. He was very exciting in the studio. He was really with us not just turn it on [snores] fall asleep. He was really with us. So he was the producer and engineer for us too and produced one of our albums, but mostly engineered. So with “Lonesome Suzie.” So a year later I’m living out in Mill Valley, California, Marin County, I get a phone call from Roy. He’s in San Francisco with Artie Garfunkel who is doing his first album, first tune, and because Roy Halee calls me, he says, “I want you to play piano to back up Artie on this first album, on a Randy Newman tune, ‘Old Man,’ about an old man dying.” A beautiful slow tune, very touching. And he said — I was totally out of shape. I am not a back-up piano player for pop people, even jazz, my time wasn’t so good. I’m much better now, twenty, thirty years later. But that’s not my thing. But he didn’t know that I was out of shape playing the piano. And I took it. So I went out there and Artie’s in another room, he’s learning the tune, he’s making mistakes, I’m privy to it, I’m sitting there. And I did about four takes on the tune. They gave me the sheet music and I played some nice Fred kind of voicings and things which were not typical for rock & roll. Slow, old man. And there were some really hip things but because we didn’t have modern equipment where you can paste together stuff we couldn’t make a version. So out of the four or five versions I didn’t come through. And I made about a thousand dollars that day, Artie took me out to Fisherman’s Wharf. I said, I didn’t need the money. I wasn’t a millionaire like him. I said, “Artie, don’t pay me.” He says, “Take the money.” It was like very authoritative. So okay. So I made a thousand dollars, double scale, blah-blah-blah you know. But the point is Roy — I said, “Why did you call me?” He says, “Your arrangement of ‘Lonesome Suzie’ is the most sensitive of any Blood, Sweat & Tears arrangement and that was my favorite arrangement. And I thought you’d be great for this tune, playing piano.”
